intro: All six of Sorrento's oldest trees stand one train stop away, in Piano di Sorrento, the neighbouring town on the same coast. Two share Villa Fondi De Sangro, a prince's garden from 1875 that is now a free public park and archaeological museum: a wide holm oak and a stone pine the WWF fought to save from pruning in 2014. Three cypresses have stood over every burial at the municipal cemetery since it opened in 1876, and a plane tree marks the last bend on the climb up to it. All free, all a short walk from the station.
meta_description: Sorrento's oldest trees, one train stop away in Piano di Sorrento: a prince's garden, three cemetery cypresses, a roadside plane, all free.
question_meta: Sorrento's oldest tree is a stone pine in Piano di Sorrento's Villa Fondi, saved from pruning by the WWF in 2014. Where it stands, and five more.
question_answer: The oldest tree associated with Sorrento is the Stone Pine of Villa Fondi, in the neighbouring town of Piano di Sorrento, one Circumvesuviana stop from Sorrento station and a ten-minute walk. Italy's national monumental-tree register and the Regione Campania's own tree card agree on its measurements exactly, 4.18 metres round and 20 metres tall, and put its age at roughly 150 years, a planting of the garden laid out in 1875 around a prince's villa. In 2014 the WWF named it and its neighbours the last old pines standing on this stretch of the tufa slope and stopped a plan to cut them back hard. A holm oak in the same park carries an identical estimated age from the same sources, so the two effectively tie; the pine gets the answer here for its fuller documented history. None of Sorrento's six oldest trees stand in Sorrento itself: all six are a short walk from the Circumvesuviana station in Piano di Sorrento, the adjoining comune on the peninsula.
question_context: This page is built on Italy's national MASAF monumental-trees register, cross-checked against the Regione Campania's own tree cards, which between them are the only two sources with any age information at all: the national data carries species and girth but no age field, so every year on this page comes from the regional card's own local testimony rather than a ring count or a planting record. All six candidates cluster in Piano di Sorrento, the town that borders Sorrento on the Sorrentine peninsula, reached by one Circumvesuviana stop and a short walk; three of them are cypresses in the same municipal cemetery, registered and dated identically by local testimony to the cemetery's 1876 opening, distinguished from each other by girth and by where the register places them on the grounds. A cluster in the grounds of the Grand Hotel Parco dei Principi was found and set aside: the hotel's own site states the garden is open to guests and restaurant patrons rather than the general public, which does not clear this site's bar for free, walk-in entry. See the full list of six on the Sorrento page.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree associated with Sorrento?
faq.a: The Stone Pine of Villa Fondi, in Piano di Sorrento, one Circumvesuviana stop from Sorrento station. It measures 4.18 metres round and is put at roughly 150 years old by both Italy's national monumental-tree register and the Regione Campania's own tree card. In 2014 the WWF named it among the last old pines on this stretch of coast and stopped a plan to prune it hard. The holm oak in the same park carries an identical age estimate.

faq.q: Are these trees actually in Sorrento?
faq.a: Not in the town itself. All six stand in Piano di Sorrento, the comune next door on the Sorrentine peninsula, reached from Sorrento station by one stop on the Circumvesuviana railway plus a walk of ten to fifteen minutes. Every entry on this page says so plainly.

Yes, all six. Villa Fondi De Sangro is a free public park run by the Comune di Piano di Sorrento; the municipal cemetery, home to all three cypresses, is open to anyone during daylight hours; the plane tree stands on an ordinary public street.

faq.q: Can I see them all in one walk?
faq.a: Yes. The holm oak and stone pine share Villa Fondi's grounds. The plane tree and the cemetery's three cypresses are a short uphill walk from there, on the road leading to the cemetery, close enough to cover with the park in one outing from the Circumvesuviana station.

trees.name: The Holm Oak of Villa Fondi

location.address: Villa Fondi De Sangro, Via Ripa di Cassano, Piano di Sorrento
location.neighbourhood: Piano di Sorrento (adjoining Sorrento, on the peninsula)

trees.story:
Three metres and eighteen centimetres round, and it stops at eleven metres tall. This holm oak spent its life spreading instead of climbing, on a terrace above Piano di Sorrento with the Bay of Naples in front of it and Vesuvius across the water.

The ground belonged to Giovanni Andrea De Sangro, Prince of Fondi, who built the villa in 1840. The garden around it was laid out in 1875. Italy's national monumental-tree register and the Regione Campania's own card for this oak agree on its measurements to the centimetre and put its age at roughly 150 years, which would make it a planting of that first garden or something a little later. Nobody has counted the rings, so the date stays an approximation, exactly as the register leaves it.

The villa passed to the comune, was restored in the 1990s and now holds the Georges Vallet archaeological museum, so the oak keeps company with Roman finds dug out of the peninsula. The park is free to walk.

One thing to expect: the two official records place this tree about 60 metres apart, both inside the same small park, so the pin gets you to the terrace rather than to the trunk. It is a short look around.

The tree is in Piano di Sorrento, not in Sorrento itself: one Circumvesuviana stop from Sorrento station, then ten minutes on foot.

trees.name: The Stone Pine of Villa Fondi

location.address: Villa Fondi De Sangro, Via Ripa di Cassano 26-34, Piano di Sorrento
location.neighbourhood: Piano di Sorrento (adjoining Sorrento, on the peninsula)

trees.story:
In 2014 the WWF called the pines of Villa Fondi the last of their kind left standing in the built-up area on the tufa slope of Piano di Sorrento, and objected to a plan to cut them back hard. The Soprintendenza confirmed the villa and its park trees were protected. The pruning did not happen.

This is the largest of them. It measures 4.18 metres round and twenty metres tall, carrying the flat spreading head that stone pines grow into once they have the room. The national register and the Regione Campania card give those figures identically and put the tree at around 150 years, presumably a planting of the garden laid out in 1875 around the De Sangro family's villa of 1840.

Its health has been a local subject. A 2020 description of the garden mentions a big pine on the sea-facing western side, put at roughly 200 years old, attacked by bark beetles and saved by dendrosurgery. Whether that account is about this exact pine is not clear: it names a different pine species than the register does, and the garden may hold more than one old specimen. Nothing on record says the registered tree has gone.

It stands in the same free public park as the holm oak, beside the Georges Vallet archaeological museum, in Piano di Sorrento. From Sorrento it is one Circumvesuviana stop and a ten-minute walk.

trees.name: The Cemetery Cypress of Piano di Sorrento

location.address: Cimitero Comunale, Via Gennaro Maresca 84, Piano di Sorrento
location.neighbourhood: Piano di Sorrento (adjoining Sorrento, on the peninsula)

trees.story:
The cemetery opened in 1876, and by the account the register recorded this cypress went into the ground the same year. It has stood over every burial the place has ever had.

That dating comes from local testimony rather than a document, which the Regione Campania card says openly; it calls the tree over 130 years old at its last update, which puts it near 150 now. Measured rather than remembered: 2.66 metres round and ten metres tall, figures the national register and the regional card give identically.

At that girth an Italian cypress reads as a column rather than the thin dark spire the species is usually planted as. Two more cypresses in this same cemetery are on the national register, at 2.70 and 3.25 metres round, so the thickest trunk you see here is not this one. Go by the coordinates instead, and give yourself a minute: the two official records for this tree sit about 90 metres apart inside the grounds.

Piano di Sorrento's municipal cemetery is a free, everyday public place, open through the daylight hours the comune sets, which shift with the season. It is a working cemetery, so the usual quiet applies.

The walk is in Piano di Sorrento rather than Sorrento: one Circumvesuviana stop from Sorrento station, then about fifteen minutes uphill on Via Gennaro Maresca.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of Via Maresca

location.address: Via Gennaro Maresca, corner Via Formiello, Piano di Sorrento
location.neighbourhood: Piano di Sorrento (adjoining Sorrento, on the peninsula)

trees.story:
The register lists this plane as a landmark rather than a specimen: it is how you know you have reached the second-to-last bend on the climb to the cemetery. A century of shade on a steep road earns a tree that job.

Local testimony recorded by the Regione Campania puts the planting at around 1920, so roughly 105 years, and nobody holds a document proving it. What is measured rather than remembered: 2.95 metres round and ten metres tall, identical in the national register and the regional card, whose coordinates land within five metres of each other. You will not have to hunt for this one.

A second plane stands beside it with a slimmer trunk, and the registered tree is the more imposing of the pair. At the last survey in 2020 its crown carried no dead stubs, which for a tree working a hot roadside on the Sorrentine peninsula is a better report than it sounds.

Via Gennaro Maresca is a public street in Piano di Sorrento, the comune next door to Sorrento, not Sorrento itself: one Circumvesuviana stop from Sorrento station, then about twelve minutes on foot uphill. Keep going for a few more minutes and you reach the cemetery cypress, which makes the two of them one short climb rather than two errands.

trees.name: The Second Cemetery Cypress of Piano di Sorrento

location.address: Cimitero Comunale, Via Gennaro Maresca 84, Piano di Sorrento
location.neighbourhood: Piano di Sorrento (adjoining Sorrento, on the peninsula)

trees.story:
Sorrento's other cemetery cypress measures 2.66 metres round. This one is thicker: 3.25 metres, the widest trunk the national register lists in Piano di Sorrento's Cimitero Comunale, registered as Cipresso n. 2 alongside two siblings.

The dating is the same local testimony that covers all three: verbal accounts place the planting in 1876, the year the cemetery itself opened, which the Regione Campania's own card repeats and calls over 130 years old at its last update, nearer 150 now. No document backs the year, only memory passed down with the ground.

At over three metres round, an Italian cypress this thick reads as a squat column rather than the narrow dark spire the species is usually planted as elsewhere on the peninsula. The two official surveys of this tree, the national register and the regional card, disagree by 25 to 30 metres on exactly where in the cemetery it stands, so the pin here is honestly approximate rather than exact.

Piano di Sorrento's municipal cemetery is free and open through the comune's daylight hours, one Circumvesuviana stop from Sorrento station and about fifteen minutes on foot up Via Gennaro Maresca, the same walk as its two sibling cypresses.

trees.name: The Third Cemetery Cypress of Piano di Sorrento

location.address: Cimitero Comunale, Via Gennaro Maresca 84, Piano di Sorrento
location.neighbourhood: Piano di Sorrento (adjoining Sorrento, on the peninsula)

trees.story:
Behind the cemetery's large chapel, at the gate on the main avenue, stands the third of Piano di Sorrento's registered cypresses: 2.70 metres round, a hand's width thicker than the smallest of the three and a metre short of the biggest.

Verbal testimony gives all three the same birth year, 1876, when the Cimitero Comunale itself opened, a dating the Regione Campania's own tree card repeats rather than independently confirms. That makes it over 130 years old at the register's last update, closer to 150 by now, the same honest caveat that applies to its two neighbours.

What sets this one apart, beyond its girth, is that it comes with an actual landmark: the register places it specifically at the gate on the main avenue behind the large chapel, rather than leaving a visitor to guess between three near-identical trunks. The two official surveys of its position agree within about five metres, tighter than either of its siblings manages, though the pin still reads approximate rather than confirmed.

Piano di Sorrento's municipal cemetery is free, open through the comune's daylight hours, one Circumvesuviana stop from Sorrento station and about fifteen minutes uphill on Via Gennaro Maresca.
